summary: Operators sometimes need an explicitly routed MPLS path to respect performance criteria such as latency, jitter and loss. This informational RFC describes how a path computation function can use network performance data, such as that advertised through TE metric extensions, when choosing the path for an RSVP-TE label switched path.

eli5.summary: Choosing a road by checking how fast and reliable it is right now, not only how short it is. This explains how network planners can do that for reserved traffic paths.

subtitle: How a path computation function can use advertised latency, jitter and loss data to pick better explicitly routed MPLS tunnels.

tldr.problem: In some networks, such as financial information networks, performance data like delay and loss matters as much as other metrics when choosing the path of an explicitly routed RSVP-TE LSP.
tldr.mechanism: A path computation function uses the per-link delay, delay variation, loss and bandwidth data from the OSPF and IS-IS TE metric extensions, either as end-to-end bounds or to exclude links, and reacts when a link is flagged Anomalous.
tldr.outcome: The document is informational. It limits the design to delay data that avoids queuing, to avoid the oscillations seen when delay was used as a routing metric before.

today: RFC 7823 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The performance data it relies on is defined in RFC 7471 for OSPF and RFC 7810 for IS-IS.

sections.title: Using Performance Data in Path Selection
sections.content:
Network performance information can come from the TE Metric Extensions in OSPF (RFC 7471) or IS-IS (RFC 7810), or from a management system. This document describes how a path computation function, whether in an ingress router or a PCE, can use that data to select paths for explicitly routed LSPs. The path may be signaled with RSVP-TE or simply used by the ingress with segment routing.

The mechanisms apply to paths fully computed at the head-end and signaled in an Explicit Route Object (ERO) where every sub-object is strict. That way the head-end can use IGP-distributed performance data without needing to signal the constraints in the RSVP Path message. Optimizing several parameters at once is computationally complex, but good heuristics exist for the delay-constrained lowest-cost (DCLC) problem, and some data can also be used to prune links before the computation.

The document does not say how a router decides which values to advertise. It assumes the rules in RFC 7471 and RFC 7810 are followed, including that queuing delay must not be included in the advertised measurements. End-to-end performance for an LSP should be built from the individual link data.
sections.eli5: Planners pick a route for important traffic by looking at how quick and steady each road is, not only how short it is.

sections.title: Requirements for the Path Computation
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven requirements for a path computation function that uses performance criteria:

  • Select a tunnel's path using existing constraints plus link latency, packet loss, jitter, conformance with link performance objectives, and bandwidth used by non-RSVP-TE traffic.
  • Allow different end-to-end performance requirements for each tunnel.
  • Periodically verify against the TE link state database that a tunnel's current LSP still meets its requirements.
  • Move tunnels with make-before-break when computed performance meets the constraints.
  • Move tunnels away from any link that violates a link performance objective.
  • Optionally avoid setting up tunnels over such a link, even if end-to-end performance would still be met.
  • Revert to the best path, using make-before-break, after a configurable period.
sections.eli5: The planners want to pick roads by speed, check from time to time that the road is still good, and switch smoothly to a better road without dropping any traffic.

sections.title: Avoiding Oscillation
sections.content:
Past attempts to use unbounded delay or loss as a routing metric suffered from severe oscillations, so performance data must be used in a way that makes undamped oscillation impossible. Timers are often cited as a cure, but oscillation damped by timers is called slosh. If advertisement timers are short relative to the jitter applied to RSVP-TE CSPF timers, partial oscillation occurs. If CSPF timers are short relative to advertisement timers, full oscillation can occur, with all traffic moving back and forth.

Jitter measurements are extremely sensitive to very low traffic levels, so any use of jitter is likely to oscillate, though some uses may be free of it. Delay measurements that are not sensitive to traffic load are safe to use, such as those made at the link layer or at a queuing priority higher than any significant traffic (for example DSCP CS7 or CS6). Measuring at the same priority as the affected traffic is likely to cause oscillation. For that reason queuing delay is excluded from the advertised values.
sections.eli5: If everyone switches roads the moment one looks faster, they all crowd onto it and it gets slow, then they all switch back. The fix is to measure in a way that crowds do not change.

sections.title: End-to-End and Link Constraints
sections.content:
The per-link data in the IGP includes unidirectional link delay, unidirectional delay variation and link loss. A CSPF can use link latency in place of TE metrics, which makes LSPs prefer the lowest-latency path. In practice, though, latency is usually a bound rather than something to minimize: the path must be no worse than the bound, not necessarily the fastest. That is the DCLC problem.

The three quantities combine differently. Path delay variation is the sum of the links' delay variations. Path loss is not a sum: the loss fraction is 1 - (1 - loss_L1)*(1 - loss_L2)*...*(1 - loss_Ln). Either can serve as an end-to-end bound.

Links can also be excluded one by one. A link that fails a test, such as having less than a minimum Unidirectional Available Bandwidth or a loss above a configurable value, is treated as if it carried a resource attribute in the exclude-any filter and is not explored.
sections.eli5: Delays add up along the way, but losses multiply: each hop only gets to deliver what the previous hop let through. A road with too little room or too many bumps is just skipped.

sections.title: Links in the Anomalous State
sections.content:
A link can stop meeting its performance objective, for example after optical regrooming or rerouting of an FA-LSP. The Anomalous bit in the Unidirectional Link Delay and Link Loss sub-TLVs signals this. If the operator does not trust such links for new LSPs, then a link with the Anomalous bit set should be removed from the topology before computing a new path, exactly as if it failed the exclude-any filter.

When the bit changes from clear to set, the ingress should scan the interested tunnels. Each should have its compliance verified, be switched to a hot standby, or do make-before-break to a secondary path, depending on configuration. The bit is only a hint: it is not sufficient on its own to decide that compliance must be checked. When a link leaves the Anomalous state, tunnels that were moved by policy may want to reoptimize to a better path, and the change helps decide when to recompute.
sections.eli5: If a road gets a warning sign, you stop sending new trips down it and check whether current trips should take another road. When the sign comes down, you may move back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that it is not currently believed to introduce new security concerns. The section contains no further text, so the document offers no additional guidance on securing the performance data.
sections.eli5: The authors do not think this adds any new ways for troublemakers to cause harm.
